inline.s: Once true faith has arisen, it must be nourished by understanding (it must be fed by understanding). Yongming says: Faith without understanding increases ignorance; understanding without faith increases wrong views. Hence we know: when faith and understanding support each other, one enters the Way swiftly. Someone asks: If one has just begun to give rise to faith but cannot yet enter the Way, is there any benefit in it? Answer: The Awakening of Faith says, if a person hears this Dharma and does not become faint-hearted, know that such a person will surely continue the Buddha’s lineage and will certainly be granted the prophecy of the Buddhas. Suppose someone could transform all the beings filling a trichiliocosm and cause them to practice the ten wholesome actions—this is not equal to a person who for a single moment rightly contemplates this Dharma; the merit of the latter surpasses the former beyond all comparison (the merit of the latter far exceeds the former’s, and cannot be fully told). Again, the Prajñā Sutras say: Even one who gives rise to pure faith for a single thought—the Tathāgata knows and sees them all, and such beings obtain immeasurable merit. From this we know: to travel a thousand li, the first step must be right; if the first step is wrong, the whole thousand li are wrong. To enter the land of the unconditioned, one’s initial faith must be right. Once initial faith is lost, all good qualities recede. Hence the patriarchs say: A hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth are set apart. This is the principle.”

[The Chan gate and the teaching gate] “The Chan gate” refers specifically to the Chan school, which transmits mind with mind; “the teaching gate” refers to all the theories and methods that come under Shakyamuni Buddha’s spoken teachings. Among the eight schools, all except Chan belong to the teaching gate. The Chan gate values understanding the mind and seeing the nature, while the teaching gate values opening the perfect understanding. [The eight schools] The Vinaya school, the Huayan school, the Tiantai school, the Sanlun school, the Faxiang school, the Zhenyan (Mantra) school, the Chan school, and the Pure Land school.
Why? Because these beings no longer have the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life; they have no mark of dharmas, and also no mark of non-dharmas.

Why do these beings obtain such immeasurable merit? Because these beings truly have faith in and understand that “all marks whatsoever are false and vain,” and so they no longer cling to the marks of a self, a human, a being, and a life as real; they do not falsely cling to the Dharma of the Way as truly existing, and still less do they deny the Dharma of the Way and falsely cling to it as nonexistent.

[The mark of dharmas] Falsely clinging to all dharmas (including the Dharma of the Way) as truly existing. [The Dharma of the Way] The dharma of cultivating the Way—that is, the dharma for ending birth and death and realizing nirvāṇa. [The mark of non-dharmas] Denying all dharmas (including the Dharma of the Way), falsely clinging to all dharmas as nonexistent, and falling into stubborn emptiness

. “Master Sengzhao says: ‘No mark of dharmas’ makes clear that dharmas are not existent, dispelling the mind that clings to existence. ‘Also no mark of non-dharmas’ makes clear that dharmas are not nonexistent, dispelling the mind that clings to nonexistence.”

(From the Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra.) [Master Sengzhao] Sengzhao, one of the four outstanding disciples of Master Kumārajīva, the translator of this sutra. [No mark of dharmas, and also no mark of non-dharmas] This says that the two extremes of existence and nonexistence are both left behind. Practicing in this way, one clings neither to dharmas nor to non-dharmas. This is to cling to neither extreme, and so to accord with the middle Way.

This sentence says: these beings will no longer cling to marks as real. This is understanding-awakening, not yet realization-awakening. Because since beginningless kalpas habit-energy has been deep-rooted and is hard to cut off all at once, though one knows in principle that “all marks whatsoever are false and vain,” when adverse or favorable conditions arise, anger and delight, right and wrong still rise again. One must, after awakening, cultivate gradually, using prajñā’s contemplation to work at removing habit, and only then can one realize awakening step by step. As it is said: “The principle may be awakened to at once; the affair must be removed gradually.”

Therefore, if this sentence were understood as “these beings no longer have the mark of a self, a human, a being, or a life, no mark of dharmas and also no mark of non-dharmas,” then these beings would already be free of all marks and would be at the level of a Buddha. (Section Fourteen says: “Free of all marks, one is then called a Buddha.”) So “these beings no longer have the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, no mark of dharmas and also no mark of non-dharmas” means that these beings have already truly come to have faith in and understand that “all marks whatsoever are false and vain,” have understood that there should no longer be the mark of a self, of a human, of a being, or of a life, or the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas, and so practice freeing themselves from marks in earnest, with this clear aim before them: no mark of a self, a human, a being, or a life; no mark of dharmas and no mark of non-dharmas.

Since beginningless kalpas, beings have taken marks to be real, and so there are the two kinds of birth-and-death (sectional birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death). Even when they study Buddhism, most cultivate while clinging to marks, seeking with a seeking mind a fruit that cannot be obtained. Now to truly have faith in and understand “no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life, no mark of dharmas and also no mark of non-dharmas,” and further to practice freeing oneself from marks in earnest—this is an immense leap. The Song of Certifying the Way says:

“Awake, and it is done—no effort is applied; / Not so with all conditioned dharmas beside. / Giving that clings to marks brings heaven’s bliss, / Like shooting arrows upward into space: / Its force once spent, the arrow falls amiss, / And future lives bring sorrow in its place. / How unlike the gate of the unconditioned Real— / One leap straight into the Tathāgata’s ground.”

Why? These beings, if their minds grasp at marks, thereby cling to a self, a human, a being, a life. If they grasp at the mark of dharmas, they cling to a self, a human, a being, a life. Why? If they grasp at the mark of non-dharmas, they cling to a self, a human, a being, a life. Therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.
Why? These beings, if their minds grasp at marks, thereby cling to a self, a human, a being, a life.”
—Why is this? Because if one falsely clings to conditions as truly existing, one thereby clings to the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life.

Why should one not grasp at the marks of conditions? If these beings’ minds grasp at marks, then who is it that grasps? It is the “I” (falsely clinging to body and mind as the self) that grasps. Once the mark of a self is established, the other three marks follow along as well (and so one clings to the four marks), and then one is lost in the dream of ignorance with no end to it. Here the World-Honored One admonishes us: do not grasp at marks.
If they grasp at the mark of dharmas, they cling to a self, a human, a being, a life.”
—By the same reasoning, if one grasps at the mark of dharmas, one clings to the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life.

By the same reasoning, who is it that grasps at the mark of dharmas? It is the “I” that grasps. Once the mark of a self is established, the other three marks follow along as well (and so one clings to the four marks), and then one is lost in the dream of ignorance with no end to it. Here the World-Honored One admonishes us: do not grasp at the mark of dharmas.
Why? If they grasp at the mark of non-dharmas, they cling to a self, a human, a being, a life.”

—Why should one not deny the Dharma of the Way? These beings, if they deny the Dharma of the Way, thereby cling to the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life.

By the same reasoning, who is it that denies the Dharma of the Way? It is the “I” that denies. Once the mark of a self is established, the other three marks follow along as well (and so one clings to the four marks), and then one is lost in the dream of ignorance with no end to it. Here the World-Honored One admonishes us: do not grasp at the mark of non-dharmas.
Therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.”

—From this the conclusion follows: “Therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.”—that is, one must neither cling to the Dharma of the Way as real, nor deny the Dharma of the Way. These are the World-Honored One’s earnest instructions to those who give rise to pure faith.

Grasping at the mark of dharmas is clinging to marks; grasping at the mark of non-dharmas is annihilating marks. Therefore one should neither cling to the Dharma of the Way nor deny it, but use it as one uses a boat—and by no means count the sands in the sea without taking the treasure. Master Yongjia’s Song of Certifying the Way says: “To sort out names and marks and never cease, / Is counting sands in the sea—self-torment without peace.”
For this reason the Tathāgata has often said: You monks should know that the Dharma I teach is like a raft. Even the Dharma should be let go, how much more so non-dharmas.

Because of this principle, I have often said: Monks, you should know that I often use a boat as a simile for all dharmas. A boat is used to cross a river; one must use it to cross, but on reaching the far shore one should let it go, and one should not, out of infatuation with this boat, refuse to let it go and go ashore. If the Dharma of the Way, which has marks but no substance (like a raft), may not be clung to and held fast, how much less may one deny the Dharma of the Way (refusing to use the raft).

Here the World-Honored One admonishes us: all dharmas are for use and must not be clung to. It is like crossing a river: one should neither refuse to let go of the raft on reaching the far shore, nor refuse to use the raft to cross. This breaks the two biased views of clinging to the existence of dharmas and clinging to their nonexistence.

[Raft] A float made of logs lashed together and used as a boat. [The Dharma is like a raft] “Dharma” here means the Dharma of the Way. The Alagaddūpama Sutra, number fifty-five in the Ahan, says: “In the mountains the water was very deep, and there was no boat or bridge. A man wished to go from this shore to the far shore, so he bound a raft and crossed over on it. Having reached the far shore, he had this thought: This raft has been of benefit to me; I cannot abandon it. I should carry it on my head and go on. What do you think—is there any benefit in the raft? The monk said: No benefit. The Buddha said: If that man were to push the raft back into the water, or leave it on the shore, what then? The monk said: That would be of benefit. The Buddha said: So it is. For your sake I have long taught the dharma of the raft simile, wishing you to abandon it, not wishing you to receive and hold it. If you know that I have long taught the dharma of the raft simile, then even that dharma may be abandoned—how much more non-dharmas?” [Non-dharmas] Denying the Dharma of the Way and falling into stubborn emptiness.

non-dharmas” has two meanings: first, denying the Dharma of the Way; second, dharmas that are not the right path. Which meaning is intended must be carefully distinguished from the context. Master Xuanzang’s translation of this passage (the Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra

Fascicle 577) reads: “Why? Subhuti! These bodhisattvas no longer have the notion of a self, the notion of a being, the notion of a life, or the notion of a receiver. These bodhisattvas have no notion of dharmas, and no notion of no-dharmas. No notion, and no no-notion. Why? Subhuti! If these bodhisattvas have a notion of dharmas, that is the grasping of a self and the grasping of a being, a life, and a receiver. Subhuti! Therefore a bodhisattva should not grasp at dharmas, nor should he grasp at non-dharmas. For this reason the Tathāgata says that if a practitioner of contemplation understands the sutra of the raft simile, even the Dharma should be abandoned—how much more non-dharmas?” From this we know that “non-dharmas” in this passage means denying the Dharma of the Way.

The World-Honored One further explains why one “should not grasp at dharmas.” Because the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Buddha-fruit is an illusion (nothing attained), and the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is likewise an illusion (nothing spoken), it is called “nothing attained, nothing spoken.”

Subhuti! What do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Does the Tathāgata speak any Dharma? Subhuti said: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can speak.

Subhuti! What do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained supreme, perfect enlightenment? Has the Tathāgata taught the sutras and spoken the Dharma? Subhuti answered: As I understand the principle the World-Honored One has stated above, that “all marks whatsoever are false and vain,” there is no truly existing dharma called supreme, perfect enlightenment, and no truly existing dharma that the Tathāgata can speak.
[Fixed dharma] Something that truly exists.
By raising these two questions the World-Honored One is testing whether Subhuti has grasped the true meaning of what was said above: “all marks whatsoever are false and vain.”
In Section Eight of this sutra the Buddha says: “What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma, and so are called Buddha and Dharma.” The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter Eleven, on the Study of Illusion, says: “The four foundations of mindfulness are not different from illusion, illusion is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness are illusion, illusion is the four foundations of mindfulness—and so on up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is illusion, illusion is anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

In Section Five the World-Honored One asked: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of bodily marks?” Subhuti knew that bodily marks are illusion, and so answered with certainty: “No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of bodily marks. Why? The bodily marks the Tathāgata speaks of are not bodily marks.” But now the World-Honored One asks: Is the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Buddha-fruit real? Is the Tathāgata’s speaking of the Dharma real? Subhuti had always taken them to be real, but since the World-Honored One had just revealed that “all marks whatsoever are false and vain,” he understood accordingly that the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Buddha-fruit is illusion and the Tathāgata’s speaking of the Dharma is also illusion; so before answering he cautiously added the phrase, “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said” (that is, as I understand the meaning of what the World-Honored One has said above).

Question: “No fixed dharma” means that there is no fixed Dharma of the Way. The World-Honored One gives medicine according to the illness; beings’ illnesses differ, and so the prescriptions differ—this is what is meant by “the Dharma has no fixed dharma.” Why, then, is “fixed dharma” explained here as “a dharma that truly exists”?

Answer: Your statement that “the World-Honored One gives medicine according to the illness; beings’ illnesses differ, and so the prescriptions differ—this is what is meant by the Dharma having no fixed dharma” is correct in itself, but it should not be applied here to explain “no fixed dharma” as “no fixed Dharma of the Way.” To do so not only fails to answer the question but also breaks the coherence of the passage. Compare the corresponding passage in the Tang

translation by Yijing: “Miaosheng (that is, Subhuti)! What do you think—has the Tathāgata attained anything with respect to supreme bodhi? And is there even a little dharma that he speaks? Miaosheng said: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, with respect to supreme bodhi the Tathāgata has in truth attained nothing, and speaks nothing.” In the Buddha Treasury Sutra
Chapter Four, on Recollecting the Saṃgha, the Buddha says: “In the ultimate meaning there is nothing fixed and real.”
Why? The Dharma the Tathāgata speaks cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken. It is not dharma, and not non-dharma.

Why is it said that “there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can speak”? Because all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever, unobtainable. Therefore the Dharma the Tathāgata speaks cannot be grasped or clung to, nor can it be put into words. The Dharma of the Way is without substance (not dharma) yet has marks (not non-dharma); therefore the Dharma of the Way is illusion.

[Cannot be grasped] One must not falsely cling to the Dharma of the Way as truly existing. [Cannot be spoken] It cannot be put into words. That Dharma of which the Tathāgata speaks cannot be expressed in words, and so it is called unspoken. The Way is in itself beyond words, yet without words it is not revealed; so it is spoken only out of sheer necessity. That is why the Tathāgata, in teaching the sutras and speaking the Dharma, must use words and language: this is pointing at the moon with a finger. But one who hears the Dharma and practices must be free of the marks of words and language, and see the moon because of the finger—that is the right path. In other words, reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma is to be guided by words and language toward realizing the Dharma that words and language can hardly express, and one must grasp the meaning beyond the words. “Cannot be spoken” here means that the Dharma of the Way spoken by the Tathāgata is a finger pointing at the moon, and is not the dharma of ultimate liberation itself. So one should not take the “finger” for the “moon,” but follow the finger to see the moon. [Not dharma, not non-dharma] “Dharma” means the Dharma of the Way. “Not dharma” says that the Dharma of the Way has no substance and must not be clung to as real; “not non-dharma” says that the Dharma of the Way has marks, and one must not cling to non-dharma either (denying the Dharma of the Way). The Dharma of the Way is an illusion with marks but no substance (all of it a matter within the dream of ignorance), and it should be used well, to leave illusion by means of illusion—crossing the river on a raft, and letting the raft go on reaching the far shore.

This passage says: the Dharma the Tathāgata speaks is in no way truly existing, nor can it be put into words; one must not cling to dharmas, nor cling to non-dharmas. Chan Master Huangbo’s Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “Dharmas are originally not existent—do not hold the view of nonexistence. Dharmas are originally not nonexistent—do not hold the view of existence. Existence (clinging to marks) and nonexistence (annihilating marks) are both views of feeling, like a cataract that breeds illusions.”
Because this passage is of vital importance for understanding and practice, I will discuss it further in detail.

The Dharma the Tathāgata speaks cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken of” has two meanings: first, one must not falsely cling to the Dharma of the Way as truly existing (“the Dharma the Tathāgata speaks cannot be grasped”), as for example one must not falsely cling to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to the Tathāgata’s speaking of the Dharma as truly existing; second, the Dharma of the Way is a finger pointing at the moon, not the moon itself (“the Dharma the Tathāgata speaks . . . cannot be spoken of”).

The Dharma the Tathāgata speaks cannot be grasped” was already explained in detail in the preceding section, when it said that one “should not grasp at dharmas (should not cling to dharmas).” As for understanding “the Dharma the Tathāgata speaks cannot be spoken of,” the simile of “finger and moon” may be used. The “finger” stands for the scriptures and teachings (what the Tathāgata speaks); the “moon” stands for the Way that the scriptures and teachings intend to point to. Practitioners should awaken to the Way through the words (the Way can be awakened to but cannot be spoken of). The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “It is like a man who points out the moon to another with his hand. That person should, because of the finger, look at the moon. But if he looks at the finger and takes it to be the body of the moon, then has this man not lost the body of the moon, and lost the finger as well? (Not only does this man fail to see the moon, he also fails to understand the meaning of the finger. This says that to falsely cling to the words of the scriptures and teachings without awakening to the Way is not only to fail to attain the Way, but also to lose the meaning of the scriptures.) Why? Because he takes the pointing finger to be the bright moon. (For the pointing finger is used to show where the moon is, and the man himself must look at the moon.)” The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “The sutra teachings (the scriptures spoken by the Tathāgata) are like a finger pointing at the moon. If one then sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed at is after all not the moon. All the various words by which all Tathāgatas instruct and reveal to bodhisattvas are likewise so.” The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says: “It is like a man who points out the moon with his finger to show a deluded person. The deluded person looks at the finger and does not look at the moon. Someone tells him: I use my finger to point at the moon so that you may know it. Why do you look at the finger and not at the moon? So it is here: words are the finger for the meaning; words are not the meaning itself.” To point at the moon with a finger is to make people leave words and language behind and awaken solely to the purport beyond words.

[Sūtra] Rendered in Chinese as “scripture,” that is, “conforming scripture.” “Conforming” means that above it conforms to the wondrous principle of all Buddhas, and below it conforms to the capacities of beings.

In studying the Dharma, what matters is to grasp the purport beyond words, and this must be realized in practice. Master Hanshan says: “When the Buddhas and patriarchs appear in the world, their thousand words and ten thousand phrases, their various skillful means, their talk of Chan and talk of doctrine, are nothing but devices that accord with capacities and break clinging (the clinging to a self and the clinging to dharmas); originally there is no real dharma to give to people.” (From the Dream Wandering Collection
Reply to Vice Censor Zheng Kunyan.)

Through words that can be spoken (the finger), one awakens to the principle they convey (the moon). Through names that can be named, one attains the essence they convey: this is to use speech to reveal the Way, and so one should understand the sutras in order to grasp their purport.

So the right attitude in studying the sutras and hearing the Dharma is: neither to take the finger for the moon, nor to discard the finger and ignore it, but to see the moon by means of the finger. In studying the teachings one should practice thus, in order to understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning. Chan Master Huangbo sighed and said: “Those who seek knowledge and views are as many as the hairs of a cow; those who awaken to the Way are as few as its horns. (A cow has countless hairs but only a pair of horns.)” The Master’s words deserve our vigilance! In the Buddha’s Forty-Two Chapter Scripture the Buddha says: “One who is widely learned and loves the Way will find the Way hard to meet; one who keeps his resolve firm and serves the Way—his Way is very great.”
Question: Why did the World-Honored One not simply bring out the “moon” whole and complete, instead of pointing at the “moon”?

Answer: Because the Way cannot be expressed in words, nor can it be inferred or imagined by the mind; it can only be realized in practice. That is why the patriarchs and great masters always say, “The path of words is cut off; the place of mental activity is extinguished,” and tell us to practice according to the teaching, to practice and realize it ourselves, and to see the moon by means of the finger. As it is said: “Like a person drinking water, who alone knows whether it is cold or warm.”

[The path of words is cut off; the place of mental activity is extinguished] If one tries to express the Way in words, the Way is cut off; if one tries to infer or imagine it with the mind, the Way is extinguished. This saying comes from the Yingluo Sutra; it means that the ultimate truth is beyond names and marks, cannot be reached by speech, cannot be known by discursive thought, and cannot be fathomed by the measure of feeling.

This section further clarifies the earlier simile of “the Dharma as a raft.” A raft is a tool for crossing a river; it cannot be left unused, but one must not falsely cling to it—one must use it correctly. Teaching the sutras and speaking the Dharma is pointing at the moon with a finger, and must be expressed in words and language; but the practice of cultivation must be free of the marks of words and language, and one must gain the moon by means of the finger—that is the right road. Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo says: “The Way is originally without words; dharmas are originally unborn. With wordless words (with the wordless word, that is, the purport beyond words) one reveals the unborn dharma, and there is no second head (do not add a head on top of a head). The moment one thinks of chasing and catching it, one has already missed it. Therefore when the patriarch came from the West, he specially proclaimed this matter. What he valued was only this: to realize it beyond words, to perceive it beyond the workings of the mind.”
To realize it beyond words, to perceive it beyond the workings of the mind” can be tasted through the following two examples:

Huike (later the Second Patriarch of Chan) said to the First Patriarch Bodhidharma: “This disciple’s mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to set it at rest.” The Patriarch said: “Bring me your mind, and I will set it at rest for you.” Huike was silent for a long while, then said: “I have sought the mind, and it cannot be found.” The Patriarch said: “I have set your mind at rest for you.” Huike was greatly awakened. (See the Five Lamps Meeting at the Source
Fascicle One.)

The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp says: “Chan Master Lingxun of Mount Furong in Fuzhou first called on Guizong (a Chan master of the Tang dynasty). He asked: What is the Buddha? Guizong said: If I tell you, will you believe it (do you really believe it)? The Master said: Since the Venerable (heshang, meaning “my teacher,” the honorific by which monks address their own teacher) speaks words of truth, how would I dare not believe? Guizong said: You yourself are it. The Master said: How should I preserve it? Guizong said: One film before the eye (falsely clinging to body and mind as the self), and flowers in the sky fall in confusion.” In these few words, seeing the nature and preserving it—the transmission of the Way was complete.

[Preserving and letting be] Preserving and letting be are the two stages of removing habit after seeing the nature. “Preserving” means doing one’s utmost to care for the holy embryo so that it suffers no harm; “letting be” means that after the holy embryo has grown to adulthood, it accords with conditions and operates naturally, being further tempered amid favorable and adverse conditions, so as to accomplish the four kinds of patience. [The four kinds of patience] The patience of submission, the patience of gentle compliance, the patience of non-arising, and the patience of still extinction. The patience of submission belongs to the beginner: wishing to endure favorable and adverse conditions, he must first tame his mind. The patience of gentle compliance comes when the mind has been tamed for a long time, so that on meeting conditions and circumstances it can endure naturally without needing to force itself—at this point the mind is gentle, good, and compliant. The patience of non-arising belongs to one on the holy levels: he understands that all dharmas are from the outset unborn, that sentient and insentient alike are produced by conditions and have no self-nature, and are empty in themselves; therefore, amid dharmas without self-nature, his enduring mind does not move, and he personally realizes non-arising. The patience of still extinction belongs to the sage at the fruit-ground: he has thoroughly realized the still-extinct realm of nirvāṇa, and both the marks of motion and of stillness accord with thusness.
Why is this so? All worthy ones and sages are distinguished by the unconditioned dharma.

The passage above said “not dharma, not non-dharma” (one must not cling to dharmas, nor cling to non-dharmas). Why is this so? Because all worthy ones and sages differ only according to the degree to which they practice freedom from marks (the unconditioned dharma).

[The unconditioned dharma] The unconditioned dharma is simply practicing while free of marks. Giving without dwelling in marks, being without the mark of a self, a human, a being, and a life, without the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas—this is the unconditioned dharma. The Treatise on the Essence of the Universe and All Things says: “The Buddha-nature is naturally so, complete in itself from the outset, pure from the outset, not produced by fabrication. It does not belong to gradual stages, does not depend on cultivation, does not await cultivation to be accomplished; its essence is of itself thus, perfect in ten thousand virtues. Understanding this naturalness, one must not give rise to a mind to fabricate, cultivate, or realize; one has only, amid conditions, not to cling and not to stall, not to let it be stained. With no dharma to be obtained and no practice to be cultivated—this is the supreme Way.” In the Buddha’s Forty-Two Chapter Scripture: “The Buddha says: The monk who leaves home cuts off desire and removes love, recognizes the source of his own mind, penetrates the Buddha’s profound principle, and understands the unconditioned dharma. Within, he has nothing to attain; without, nothing to seek. His mind is not tied to the Way (he does not cling to the Way), nor does he bind up karma (nor does he create karma). Without thought, without doing; neither cultivating nor realizing (cultivating without cultivating, realizing without realizing). He does not pass through the various stages (he does not pass through the fifty-two stages), and yet is himself the most honored—this is called the Way.” The words “he does not pass through the various stages, and yet is himself the most honored” show that the unconditioned dharma is the practice of the One Vehicle (the Buddha Vehicle). The Diamond Sutra is the Dharma of the supreme vehicle, and so it teaches the unconditioned dharma of neither cultivating nor realizing—all dharmas are false and vain; not receiving, not thinking; no grasping, no rejecting; no seeking, no clinging. For example, in Section Three the Buddha says, “Thus I liberate immeasurable, countless, boundless beings, and yet no being has been liberated,” and in Section Four the Buddha says, “give without dwelling in marks”—these are the unconditioned dharma. [The conditioned dharma] The conditioned dharma is practicing while clinging to marks. In Section Fourteen the Buddha says: “If the bodhisattva’s mind dwells in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man who enters the darkness and sees nothing. If the bodhisattva’s mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man with eyes, illumined by the light of the sun, seeing all the various colors.” Here giving stands for the six perfections and myriad practices. The six perfections and myriad practices practiced with clinging to marks are the conditioned dharma; practiced free of marks, they are the unconditioned dharma.

Freedom from marks—this is the guiding principle and outline of this sutra. Why must one be free of marks? Because “all marks whatsoever are false and vain. If one sees all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathāgata.” (Section Five) And further, “Free of all marks, one is then called a Buddha.” (Section Fourteen) All marks can be gathered into six great categories: the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, the mark of a life, and the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas—that is, the clinging to a self and the clinging to dharmas. In this sutra, through his dialogue with Subhuti, the World-Honored One again and again breaks them one by one. In Sections Three and Four he breaks the four marks; in Section Six, by the simile of the raft, he breaks the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas. In this section, that the Tathāgata attains nothing and the Tathāgata speaks nothing breaks the mark of dharmas.
Question: “The unconditioned dharma” means dharmas that are not produced by causes and conditions. Why is “the unconditioned dharma” explained here as practicing free of marks?

Answer: The term “unconditioned dharma” has two meanings. First, in Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s Treatise on the Door of Understanding the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna, all dharmas are summarized into one hundred categories, called the hundred dharmas; of these, ninety-four are dharmas produced by causes and conditions, collectively called conditioned dharmas, and the remaining six are dharmas not produced by causes and conditions, collectively called unconditioned dharmas. Here “dharma” means things and phenomena—that “dharma.” “The unconditioned dharma” has yet another meaning: the unconditioned dharma spoken of in this passage, “all worthy ones and sages are distinguished by the unconditioned dharma,” which is also the unconditioned dharma spoken of in the Buddha’s Forty-Two Chapter Scripture: “The Buddha says: The monk who leaves home cuts off desire and removes love, recognizes the source of his own mind, penetrates the Buddha’s profound principle, and awakens to the unconditioned dharma.”

In the following translations, the “unconditioned dharma” of this passage as translated by Master Kumārajīva is rendered “the unconditioned,” which shows that “the unconditioned dharma” here does not mean dharmas not produced by causes and conditions:
The Tang
translation by Yijing: “Why? The Dharma spoken by the Buddha cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken; it is not dharma, not non-dharma. Why? Because all sages are what the unconditioned manifests.”
The Tang

translation by Xuanzang: “Why, World-Honored One? The dharma realized, spoken, and contemplated by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, cannot be grasped and cannot be proclaimed; it is not dharma, not non-dharma. Why? Because all worthy and sage persons are what the unconditioned manifests.”
[Pudgala] Another name for “beings.”

blocks.text: Section 8: The Dharma Born of This Sutra

inline.s: This section shows that this sutra is the dharma by which one becomes a Buddha. The “Dharma” in “the Dharma born of this sutra” refers to the Dharma of the Way taught in this sutra. “Born of” refers to what the text of this section says: “All Buddhas, and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, come forth from this sutra.”

Subhuti! What do you think? If a person filled a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and used them in giving, would the merit that person obtains be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? This merit is not the nature of merit; therefore the Tathāgata says the merit is great.
Subhuti! What do you think? If a person filled a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and used them in giving, would the merit that person obtains be great?”

—The World-Honored One asks: Subhuti! What do you think? If someone gives in charity the seven treasures in such quantity as to fill a trichiliocosm, is the merit that person obtains not very great indeed?

[Trichiliocosm] That is, a great thousandfold world; it is the region taught and transformed by one Buddha. One Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents is called a small world. One thousand small worlds gathered together is called a small thousandfold world; one thousand small thousandfold worlds is called a middling thousandfold world; one thousand middling thousandfold worlds is called a great thousandfold world. Because “thousand” is said three times, a great thousandfold world is also called a “trichiliocosm.” [Mount Sumeru] Rendered in Chinese as Wondrous High Mountain, it is the center of a small world. This mountain is made of the four treasures gold, silver, beryl, and crystal; no other mountain can compare with its height, and it is the king of mountains. [The four great continents] Around Mount Sumeru there are four great continents: the eastern one is called Pūrvavideha, the southern one is called Jambudvīpa (the world we live in is on this continent), the western one is called Aparagodānīya, and the northern one is called Uttarakuru. [The seven treasures] Gold, silver, beryl, crystal (similar to rock crystal; two thousand years ago there was not yet what we now call glass), tridacna shell, red pearl, and carnelian. [Would it not be very great?] Is it not very great indeed? [Would it not] Is it not.
Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? This merit is not the nature of merit; therefore the Tathāgata says the merit is great”

—Subhuti answered: Very great indeed, World-Honored One! Why? This merit is not a truly existing entity but an illusion, a matter within the dream of ignorance. Precisely because merit is an illusion can there be any talk of its being much or little (for “much” and “little” are concepts within the dream of ignorance); therefore the Tathāgata says this merit is great.

[Not the nature of merit] The Record of the Doctrine of Consciousness-Only says: “Nature means substance.” Merit is a matter within the dream of ignorance, having marks but no substance. “Not the nature of merit” says that merit is not truly existing but an illusion.

If again there is a person who receives and upholds this sutra, even a four-line verse of it, and expounds it for others, his merit surpasses that. Why? Subhuti! All Buddhas, and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, come forth from this sutra. Subhuti! What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma, and so are called Buddha and Dharma.

Note: The last sentence of this passage in the current circulated text reads: “Subhuti! What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma, and so are called Buddha and Dharma.” In the Qianlong edition of the Buddhist canon, the four characters “and so are called Buddha and Dharma” do not appear. However, in the Chen
Paramārtha translation it reads: “Subhuti! What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma, and so are called Buddha and Dharma.” In the Tang

Xuanzang translation it reads: “Subhuti! As for Buddhas and dharmas, Buddhas and dharmas—the Tathāgata says they are not Buddhas and dharmas; therefore the Tathāgata speaks of Buddhas and dharmas, Buddhas and dharmas.” In the Tang
Yijing translation it reads: “Therefore, Miaosheng! Buddha and Dharma—the Tathāgata says they are not Buddha and Dharma, and so are called Buddha and Dharma.”
If again there is a person who receives and upholds this sutra, even a four-line verse of it, and expounds it for others, his merit surpasses that”

—The World-Honored One says: If there is another person who receives and upholds all of this sutra, or a part of it, or even only a single verse (four lines), and expounds it for others, the merit he obtains surpasses the merit obtained by the person before who gave in charity the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm.
This sentence breaks the mark of non-dharmas.

[Verse (gāthā)] “Gāthā” is the short form of “gāthā”; it is a kind of rhymed composition somewhat like poetry, usually taking four lines as one verse. A verse is the basic unit of a sutra, and the size of a sutra is usually indicated by how many verses it contains; for example, the Zhenyuan Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings

Fascicle Seventeen says: “The Sanskrit text of the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra has altogether six bundles, a total of one hundred thousand verses.” Here “a four-line verse” refers generally to any four lines in the sutra. Someone asked Master Hanshan: What exactly are the four lines of the Diamond Sutra? The great masters of old each spoke differently, and there is no fixed answer. Why? The Master answered: “The prajñā spoken by the Buddha is like the many grasses on a snow mountain—every one of them is medicine; pick one up and use it, and it will certainly cure the illness. So when the ancients pointed out what the four lines are, each was picking one stalk of grass from the snow mountain.” (From the Dream Wandering Collection

Eight Requests for Instruction from Jizhao Kaigong.) [The many grasses of the snow mountain] On the snow mountain there is a wondrous herb; those who see it gain immeasurable life. The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “In the snow mountain there is a supreme fragrant medicine named sāhā; those who see it gain immeasurable life and are free of illness and suffering.”

[Receiving and upholding] “Receiving” is accepting: through understanding the principle and the Dharma of the Way in the sutra, one gives rise to faith, and so accepts it sincerely. “Upholding” is putting it into practice: one acts in accord with the principle and the Dharma of the Way in the sutra. As it is said: understand the sutra and attain the Dharma; practice according to the Dharma. [Receiving and upholding even a four-line verse, and expounding it for others] Either receiving and upholding the whole, or a part, or even only a single verse (four lines), and expounding it for others.
Why? Subhuti! All Buddhas, and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, come forth from this sutra”

—Why is it that receiving and upholding the Diamond Sutra, even a four-line verse of it, and expounding it for others, brings such great merit? Subhuti! Because this sutra is the mind-dharma of all Buddhas: all Buddhas attain the Way by relying on this sutra, and the dharma by which Buddhas become Buddhas comes forth from this sutra.
Question: Why is it said that “all Buddhas, and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, come forth from this sutra”?
Answer: On this question the layman Jiang Weinong, in his
Lectures on the Diamond Sutra
, gives a most penetrating exposition:
“In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, what matters is to be deeply watchful and sober
(cautious and fearful)
, taking what the Buddha says as a mirror, at all times and in all places using it to reflect upon oneself
(to compare whether one’s body, speech, and mind accord with what the Buddha says; where they accord, that is awakening; where they do not accord, that is delusion)

. If one does not observe and does not reflect, how can delusion become awakening? This is what is meant by relying on the words to give rise to contemplation. When the work of contemplation has long been established, then a grave and watchful mind arises of itself—this is initial awakening, and it is also the first opening of the right wisdom inherent in the principle-essence. If one does not retreat and does not slacken, the work of contemplation grows deeper and purer day by day. Then what is called initial awakening is first like the new moon: gradually the light waxes and the darkness
(here the same as “dark”)

wanes, until the moon’s disk is full and its radiance shines forth, and the essence of the nature appears. This is initial awakening merging with original awakening, and there is no longer any division of initial and original. You should know that what is called becoming a Buddha is nothing else: the awakening nature perfectly bright. And the opening of the awakening nature cannot come about except by relying on the power of the prajñā of words. Therefore it is said: All Buddhas come forth from this sutra.”
Subhuti! What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma, and so are called Buddha and Dharma”
—Subhuti! What are called Buddha and Dharma (having marks) are not Buddha and Dharma (having no substance), and so are called Buddha and Dharma (being illusions).
This sentence breaks the mark of dharmas. The view of a Buddha and the view of dharmas are gone—how much less could there arise the afflicted view of beings?

[Buddha and Dharma] In this sentence, “Buddha” refers to “all Buddhas” in the sentence above, “all Buddhas, and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, come forth from this sutra”; “Dharma” refers to “the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas” in this sentence.

As for the Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi being illusions, the Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky.” It also says: “Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are alike the mark of a sky-flower.” The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “There is no Buddha of nirvāṇa, and no nirvāṇa of a Buddha.” The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra
Chapter Three, on Practicing in Accord, the Buddha says: “There is no Buddha and also no Buddha Way.” The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter Eleven, on the Study of Illusion, says: “The four foundations of mindfulness are not different from illusion, illusion is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness are illusion, illusion is the four foundations of mindfulness—and so on up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is illusion, illusion is anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” In Section Seventeen of this sutra the Buddha says: “Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Shakyamuni. Because in truth there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dīpaṃkara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Shakyamuni.”

This section says that the merit of receiving and upholding this sutra is inconceivable, because this one fascicle of the Diamond Sutra is the mind-dharma of all Buddhas: all Buddhas, and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, come forth from this sutra.

Before this, the World-Honored One had all along been breaking beings’ false view of clinging to the scriptures and teachings, but he also feared that beings might go to the other extreme—denying and slighting the scriptures, the teachings, and the Buddha-Dharma, and falling into the dark abyss of ignorance. So here he says: the merit of upholding the sutra is inconceivable, and all Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra. Yet again, fearing that beings might falsely cling to this as real, he once more reminds them: “What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma, and so are called Buddha and Dharma.” Truly his words are earnest and his heart kind—again and again, time after time, he patiently guides us beings, telling us neither to cling to marks nor to annihilate marks, but to be good at using the false to cultivate the true, to leave illusion by means of illusion, until illusion is exhausted and the dream ends.

Question: The Diamond Sutra says, “All marks whatsoever are false and vain.” The Complete Enlightenment Sutra also says, “All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky.” Since the Buddha-worlds are illusion, why should one still seek birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Answer: If in this life we could be free of all marks, become Buddhas, and leave the dream, that would of course be best—but we cannot do it. Even a bodhisattva of the initial stage of faith must pass through fifty-two stages and three great asamkhyeya kalpas before he can become a Buddha and leave the dream of ignorance. Although each stage is still illusion, each is closer to the goal of leaving the dream than the last; this is to leave illusion by means of illusion, until illusion is exhausted and the dream ends. The three realms are like a burning house: though they are illusion, the knowing mind is not yet exhausted and one is still within the dream, with the keenly felt pain of birth, aging, sickness, and death—truly a suffering beyond words, tormented through and through! Moreover, once the human body is lost, it is hard to regain it for ten thousand kalpas, and when one might hear the Buddha-Dharma again, who knows in what age that would be! So the first step is: in this very life one must escape from the three realms of birth-and-death and rebirth.

We are now in the age of the Dharma’s end, and the practical road is to recite the Buddha’s name and seek birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Great Collection Sutra says: “In the age of the Dharma’s end, among hundreds of billions of people who cultivate, scarcely one attains the Way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation can one cross over birth and death.” Mazu founded the monasteries (Chan temples), and Baizhang established the pure rules. Chan Master Baizhang Dazhi’s “Essential Rules of the Monastery” (in those days it was not yet the age of the Dharma’s end, and so many people accomplished the Way through Chan practice) begins by saying: “A monastery flourishes through having no affairs; in practice, Buddha-recitation is the safe and sure way.” For the ordinary path of ending birth and death requires cutting off the afflictions of view and thought, whereas to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one need only suppress the afflictions—compared with the former this is far, far easier. Therefore in practice, Buddha-recitation is the safe and sure way.

In addition, even if the afflictions of view and thought are exhausted and one can by one’s own power end sectional birth-and-death, still, once out of the three realms there remains an extremely long road to travel in ending transformational birth-and-death. In the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one has not only ended sectional birth-and-death but also possesses the best conditions for study and practice in order to end transformational birth-and-death: Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva are one’s guides, the great bodhisattvas are one’s fellow practitioners, and one may go to the places of the Buddhas of the ten directions to study. Moreover, the Buddha Speaks of Amitābha Sutra says: “In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all beings born there are avaivartika.” Avaivartika means non-retrogression—not to be disturbed by any māra, and never to fall back, until Buddhahood. This is the name of a bodhisattva stage, reaching which requires one great asamkhyeya kalpa of practice; yet we need only be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss to reach this stage and never again fall back. That is why, in the Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Practices and Vows of the Avataṃsaka Sutra, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s ten kings of vows (the most supreme among vows are called kings of vows) guide all back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss: “By this supreme practice of Samantabhadra, / All boundless victory and blessing I dedicate: / May all beings drowning in the sea of suffering / Quickly go to the realm of the Buddha of Infinite Light.” Amitābha Buddha is also named the Buddha of Infinite Light, and the realm of the Buddha of Infinite Light is the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Here we should carefully realize the World-Honored One’s instruction in Section Six: “One should not grasp at non-dharmas.” By no means should one decline to board the jewel ship and instead try to swim the sea alone. Therefore Chan Master Zhongfeng says: “The sea of awakening gives the void its birth; / Through Sahā’s contrary waves it flows on earth. / Whoever would reach the farther shore / In Ultimate Bliss has a boat for home.” Once we arrive in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there is a great jewel dharma-ship that carries us smoothly and swiftly to the farther shore of nirvāṇa; and then we return into the sea of suffering in lands as numerous as dust-motes, to liberate all beings of the dharma-realm far and wide.
On this question the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Chan Master Chewu, gives a most penetrating instruction (see the Bequeathed Collected Works of Chan Master Chewu

Fascicle One): “A Chan practitioner asked: All dharmas are like a dream. Sahā is certainly a dream, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is also a dream. Since both are the same one dream, what benefit is there in cultivating it? I (Chan Master Chewu) said: Not so! Before the seventh ground, one cultivates the Way within a dream. In the great dream of ignorance, even one at equal enlightenment still sleeps. Only the Buddha alone is first called the Greatly Awakened. When the dream-eye has not yet opened, suffering and joy are plainly there. Rather than suffer the utmost suffering of Sahā in a dream, why not enjoy the wondrous joy of Ultimate Bliss in a dream? Moreover, the dream of Sahā is to pass from dream into dream, dreaming on and on, sinking ever deeper; the dream of Ultimate Bliss is to pass from dream into awakening, awakening on and on, gradually reaching the great awakening. Though the dream is the same, what dreams it is not at all the same! How can they be lumped together?”

[Chan Master Chewu] A man of the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns of the Qing dynasty, named Jixing, styled Chewu. He was greatly awakened through Chan practice and was the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji lineage. He had long admired the life of Chan Master Yongming Yanshou, and so turned his mind to the Pure Land and upheld the Lotus school. Each day he set a limit of one stick of incense for meeting guests; beyond that he only bowed and recited. Whenever the Master taught the Dharma, it poured forth like a bottle emptied, like clouds rising, with unobstructed eloquence; the style of the Lotus school spread widely, and he became the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school. The Master knew beforehand the time of his passing: on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the fifteenth year of Jiaqing, facing west and joining his palms, he sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name, saw the Buddha descend to receive him, and passed away; the assembly smelled a rare fragrance floating in the air. He was enshrined for seven days, his countenance as if alive, kind and full; his white hair turned black, and his complexion was extraordinarily radiant.

[The seventh ground] From ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment (when the stage of wondrous enlightenment is complete, one becomes a Buddha). The seventh of the ten grounds is called “the seventh ground.” [Equal enlightenment] Among the fifty-two stages, the fifty-first is called equal enlightenment: a bodhisattva who has completed the ten grounds and is about to realize the Buddha-fruit, whose merit and wisdom are nearly equal to a Buddha’s, and so is called “equal enlightenment.”

Question: In reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, a great master says, “As to birth, one is certainly born; as to going, one in truth does not go.” How should this be understood?

Answer: The saying “As to birth, one is certainly born; as to going, one in truth does not go” comes from Master Yihuai of the Song dynasty. The Master was a dharma-heir of Chongxian, the reviving patriarch of the Yunmen school; throughout his life he directed his merit toward the Pure Land, and he wrote the Treatise Resolving Various Doubts about the Pure Land. “As to birth, one is certainly born” means: being born there means the consciousness goes to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and is no longer subject to birth-and-death and rebirth—this truly happens and is not unreal. “As to going, one in truth does not go” means: being born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is likewise a matter within the dream of ignorance, and its essence is not truly existing; hence “in truth does not go.” This is also the principle taught in the next section, Section Nine, “One Mark, No Marks,” for example: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can a sakṛdāgāmin think, ‘I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin’? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? A sakṛdāgāmin is called a once-returner, yet in truth there is no coming or going; therefore he is called a sakṛdāgāmin.” The Lectures on the Diamond Sutra says: “You should know that when Amitābha comes to receive one, he has never actually come; and being born in the West, one has never actually gone. Though one has never gone, what prevents appearing to come and appearing to go? Why? That which neither comes nor goes is the principle-essence; that which has coming and going is the mark of affairs. Principle and affair have never been two; nature and mark must be perfectly fused. Therefore, though it is neither coming nor going, this does not hinder there being coming and going; and though there is coming and going, in truth it is neither coming nor going. Most important: coming and going must be realized upon that which neither comes nor goes, and that which neither comes nor goes must be brought forth amid coming and going. This is the essential secret of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth there. Having gained this essential secret, one will certainly be born there and see the Buddha. Who says that cultivating the Pure Land requires no study of prajñā, and even suspects that prajñā obstructs the Pure Land?”

This section says: even one who has realized a fruit does not think that he has attained a fruit; thus should one be free of marks. Here the World-Honored One takes the four fruits that Subhuti himself realized (the fruit of a srota-āpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, and the fruit of an arhat) as examples to break the mark of dharmas, which makes it all the more intimate.

[One mark, no marks] This says that all marks are illusions (“all marks whatsoever are false and vain”), and their essence is one single mark (one mark)—nothing whatsoever; this is no marks. It is just as one who dreams sees the affairs of a dream in all their variety, with all kinds of marks; but for one whose eyes are awake there is nothing whatsoever, and this single mark of nothing whatsoever is no marks. The Buddha says: “All dharmas have but one mark, which is called no marks.” (The Buddha Treasury Sutra
Chapter One, on the True Character of All Dharmas)

What precedes speaks of non-dwelling—not dwelling in marks, because “all marks whatsoever are false and vain.” This section speaks of the cultivation of no marks—the unconditioned dharma—which is a further stage of skill. Above, the World-Honored One said that the Buddha-fruit he himself realized cannot be obtained; in this section he says: Subhuti, the fruit you have realized also cannot be obtained—“no srota-āpanna, no fruit of a srota-āpanna; no sakṛdāgāmin, no fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin; no anāgāmin, no fruit of an anāgāmin; no arhat, no fruit of an arhat.”
In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter Three, on Practicing in Accord, the Buddha says: “Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formation, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mental consciousness; no ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, its cause, its cessation, or its path; no wisdom and no attainment; no srota-āpanna, no fruit of a srota-āpanna, no sakṛdāgāmin, no fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, no anāgāmin, no fruit of an anāgāmin, no arhat, no fruit of an arhat, no pratyekabuddha, no way of the pratyekabuddha; no Buddha, and no Buddha Way. Shariputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus practices in accord, this is called according with the perfection of prajñā.”
Some of the terms here need explanation to make the following text easier to understand; readers already familiar with these names and marks may skip at once.

[Mahāyāna] That is, the gate of the bodhisattva, whose guiding purpose is to save the world and benefit others, and whose highest fruit is the Buddha-fruit. From ordinary being to Buddhahood the Mahāyāna has fifty-two stages, namely: the ten stages of faith (“ten” indicates that ten stages are contained; the same applies below), the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment (the Buddha-fruit). “Vehicle” means that which carries, a simile for the Buddha-Dharma as a ferryboat that can carry beings from this shore of birth-and-death to the farther shore of nirvāṇa. The bodhisattva vehicle liberates many beings, and so is called the Great Vehicle; the śrāvaka vehicle and the pratyekabuddha vehicle liberate few beings, and so are called the Small Vehicle. [The Small Vehicle] The gate of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, whose guiding purpose is to cultivate the self and benefit oneself. [The śrāvaka vehicle] Those who, hearing the Buddha’s voice and cultivating the four noble truths, awaken to the Way. The śrāvaka vehicle has four fruits: the fruit of a srota-āpanna (first fruit), the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin (second fruit), the fruit of an anāgāmin (third fruit), and the fruit of an arhat (fourth fruit). To realize the fruit of an arhat is to end birth-and-death and leave the three realms. [The pratyekabuddha vehicle] The pratyekabuddha vehicle is also called the middle vehicle; it cultivates the twelve links of dependent origination, and its highest fruit is the fruit of a pratyekabuddha. From ordinary being to pratyekabuddha, its cultivation places weight on awakening and realization; wherever the awakening reaches, there the realization reaches, and so there are no clear stages to speak of. [The four noble truths] Also called the four truths of the sages, namely the truth of suffering, the truth of its cause, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path (abbreviated as suffering, cause, cessation, and path); “truth” means ultimate reality. The truth of suffering explains the truth that human life is full of suffering; in the truth of its cause, “cause” means that which gathers—it explains the truth of how the suffering of human life comes about; the truth of cessation explains the truth that only the realm of nirvāṇa is the final ending of suffering; the truth of the path explains the truth of how one must cultivate the Way in order to realize nirvāṇa. These four noble truths include within them the two layers of cause and effect of the world and beyond the world: cause is the cause and suffering is the fruit—this is the cause and effect of the deluded realm; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit—this is the cause and effect of the awakened realm. [The twelve links of dependent origination] These explain the process by which sentient beings flow through birth-and-death. The twelve links are: ignorance (the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion, which are the root of birth-and-death), formation (the creating of karmas), consciousness (the karmic consciousness entering a womb), name-and-form (when there is only a fetal form and the six faculties are not yet complete), the six sense-gates (when the fetus has grown into a human form with the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), contact (emerging from the womb and coming into contact with outer conditions), feeling (on contact with outer conditions, giving rise to feelings of suffering and pleasure), craving (giving rise to desire for conditions), grasping (seeking and acting), becoming (forming karmic causes that can bring about future retribution), birth (again receiving a future body of the five aggregates), and aging-and-death (the future body gradually aging and dying). These twelve links include all the causes and effects of the three times—the arising of delusion, the creating of karma, and the receiving of birth—turning around and around without end.

[The five aggregates] Form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness—these are the five great elements that make up the human person. Among them, the aggregate of form (matter) is the body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness) are the mind. The five aggregates were formerly translated as the five shadows. The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “At the time of death, relatives weep. The person is terrified and cannot master himself. All the good and evil of his life appear before him. After the warmth is gone, the past five shadows cease and the present intermediate existence arises. After entering the womb, the present intermediate existence ceases and the future five shadows arise. It is like a lamp lighting as darkness is extinguished, and the lamp going out as darkness arises, continuing without interruption.” [Feeling] When the faculty and its object touch, the mental function arises of feelings such as suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. [Perception] Depending on feeling, the imagining of things arises, or the choosing to take up or reject, to welcome or refuse. [Formation] Depending on imagining and choosing, the mental function arises of good and evil actions. [Consciousness] The discerning and knowing of the objects of the corresponding realm.

[The world and beyond the world] The world and what is beyond the world. The world is the realm of ordinary beings in the six paths (hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and gods); beyond the world is the realm of arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. [The two afflictions] The afflictions of view and the afflictions of thought. The afflictions of view are wrong views, such as the five wrong views of the view of a body, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions. The afflictions of thought, also called the afflictions of cultivation, are the afflictions of matters such as greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. Cutting off these two afflictions of view and thought is to realize the fruit of an arhat and leave the three realms. Furthermore, the afflictions of view are intellectual afflictions, cut off at the time of seeing the Way, and so are also called “what is abandoned by seeing”; the afflictions of thought are habitual afflictions that are born with one, and must be cut off through long cultivation, and so are also called “what is abandoned by cultivation.” [The five wrong views] Also called the five evil views: the view of a body, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions. “The view of a body” is clinging to the body falsely combined of the five aggregates as truly existing. “Extreme views” are evil views that lean to one side; for example, some people think that after death everything returns to nothing—as when a person dies, it is like a lamp going out—and this is called the view of annihilation; others think that after death one is still a human, and that pigs, horses, cattle, and sheep after death are still pigs, horses, cattle, and sheep, and this is called the view of permanence. The views of clinging to annihilation and to permanence both lean to one side, and so are called extreme views. “Wrong views” are views that are false and not right, such as denying cause and effect, and destroying all good deeds. “The view of grasping at views” is to cling to the three wrong views above (the view of a body, extreme views, and wrong views) as correct. “The view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions” is to uphold wrong precepts and mistake them for right precepts, as when some people smear themselves with ash (the ash-smearing sect was one of the ancient Indian sects: they smear their whole bodies with ash and seek rebirth in heaven through austerities) and fast, mistakenly thinking this is the way of liberation.

Subhuti! What do you think? Can a srota-āpanna think, ‘I have attained the fruit of a srota-āpanna’? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? A srota-āpanna is called a stream-enterer, and yet he enters nothing—he does not enter form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; therefore he is called a srota-āpanna.

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can a person of the first fruit think, “I have attained the fruit of a srota-āpanna”? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! Why? Because the srota-āpanna is called a stream-enterer (one who enters the stream of the sages) precisely because he enters nothing (he is free of marks) and does not enter the six dusts (he can empty the feelings and consciousness, and be free of the marks of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas); therefore he is called a srota-āpanna. If he still clung to marks and thought there was something entered (thinking he had gained something in practice), then he would not be called a srota-āpanna.

[Srota-āpanna] Rendered in Chinese as “stream-enterer,” meaning one who has just entered the stream of the sages, because he has already cut off all the afflictions of view; at most he will be born seven times back and forth among humans and gods, and will certainly realize the fruit of an arhat.

The Buddha’s Forty-Two Chapter Scripture says: “An arhat can fly and transform himself, has a lifespan of vast kalpas, and his staying or moving shakes heaven and earth. Next is the anāgāmin. The anāgāmin, when his life ends, has his spirit (consciousness) go up to the nineteenth heaven and realizes arhatship. Next is the sakṛdāgāmin. The sakṛdāgāmin, by one going up and one coming back, attains arhatship. Next is the srota-āpanna. The srota-āpanna, by seven deaths and seven births, then realizes arhatship.”

Subhuti! What do you think? Can a sakṛdāgāmin think, ‘I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin’? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? A sakṛdāgāmin is called a once-returner, yet in truth there is no coming or going; therefore he is called a sakṛdāgāmin.

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can a person of the second fruit think, “I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin”? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! Why? Because although the sakṛdāgāmin must go once to the heavens and come once to the human realm in order to cut off the afflictions of thought and realize the fruit of an arhat, all this is a matter within the dream of ignorance, and so in truth there is no coming or going; therefore he is called a sakṛdāgāmin.

[Sakṛdāgāmin] Rendered in Chinese as “once-returner.” The afflictions of thought (greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt) are the subtlest, are born with one, and are divided into ten grades. After a cultivator has cut off all the afflictions of view and realized the first fruit, he cuts off the first six grades of the afflictions of thought and realizes the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin). After that he must still go once to the heavens and come once to the human realm, continuing to cut off the afflictions of thought in order to realize the third fruit (anāgāmin), and then in the four dhyāna heavens of the form realm he cuts off the afflictions of thought entirely and realizes the fourth fruit (arhat). In sum, it is by one going to the heavens and one coming to the human realm that he realizes the fruit of an arhat, and so he is called a “once-returner.”

Subhuti! What do you think? Can an anāgāmin think, ‘I have attained the fruit of an anāgāmin’? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? An anāgāmin is called a non-returner, yet in truth there is no non-returning; therefore he is called an anāgāmin.

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can a person of the third fruit think, “I have attained the fruit of an anāgāmin”? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! Why? Because although the anāgāmin is called a non-returner (not returning to be born in the human realm), all this is a matter within the dream of ignorance, and so in truth there is no non-returning; therefore he is called an anāgāmin.

[Anāgāmin] Rendered in Chinese as “non-returner.” After a cultivator realizes the second fruit, he cuts off three more grades of the afflictions of thought and realizes the third fruit. One who reaches this fruit dwells in the four dhyāna heavens of the form realm, realizes the fruit of an arhat there, and does not again return to be born in the human realm; therefore he is called a “non-returner.”

Subhuti! What do you think? Can an arhat think, ‘I have attained the way of an arhat’? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? In truth there is no dharma called an arhat. World-Honored One! If an arhat thinks, ‘I have attained the way of an arhat,’ then he clings to a self, a human, a being, and a life.

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can a person of the fourth fruit think, “I have attained the fruit of an arhat”? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! Why? Because the dharma “named arhat” (the mark of the affair) is not truly existing. If an arhat still had the thought that he had attained the fruit of an arhat, he would be falsely clinging to all dharmas as real (clinging to a self, a human, a being, and a life), and he would not be an arhat.

[Arhat] Rendered in Chinese as “non-arising.” After a cultivator realizes the third fruit, in the four dhyāna heavens he cuts off the last grade of the afflictions of thought; the afflictions are exhausted, and he does not receive further existence (when an arhat’s afflictions and karmas of birth-and-death are exhausted, he no longer receives a body in a later life, and so it is said that he “does not receive further existence”). Birth-and-death are ended from then on, and so it is called “non-arising”; this is the highest fruit of the śrāvaka vehicle. [Attaining the way of an arhat] Attaining the fruit of an arhat. The Chen

Paramārtha translation reads: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can an arhat think: I have attained the fruit of an arhat?” [In truth there is no dharma called an arhat] This sentence means: there truly is no such affair as “there being a dharma named arhat.” That is to say, “there being a dharma named arhat” is a matter within the dream of ignorance and is not truly existing. Subhuti says: realizing the fruit of an arhat is an illusion and not truly existing, and at the same time he himself does not have the thought of having attained arhatship (he does not cling to the mark of arhat). This is the cultivation of no marks, what is called “cultivating without cultivating.” “Cultivating” means applying effort; “without cultivating” means not clinging to the mark of cultivation. Cultivation is to turn delusion into awakening, and clinging to marks is itself delusion; therefore cultivation that clings to marks cannot succeed—as it is said, boiling sand does not make rice. The cultivation of no marks is the unconditioned dharma; cultivation that clings to marks is the conditioned dharma.

World-Honored One! The Buddha says that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention, that I am foremost among men, that I am the foremost arhat free of desire. World-Honored One! I do not think, “I am an arhat free of desire.” World-Honored One! If I thought, “I have attained the way of an arhat,” the World-Honored One would not say that Subhuti delights in the practice of araṇya. Because Subhuti in truth practices nothing, he is called one who delights in the practice of araṇya.

Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! The Buddha says that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention, that I am foremost among men, the foremost arhat free of desire. But I do not think thus, that I am an arhat free of desire, and still less would I think that I am the foremost arhat free of desire. World-Honored One! If I thought thus, that I had realized the fruit of an arhat, the Buddha would not say that Subhuti is a cultivator who delights in the practice of non-contention. It is precisely because Subhuti does not cling to marks or fabricate, and has no discriminating mind of attainment or non-attainment, that the Buddha says Subhuti is a cultivator who delights in the practice of non-contention.

[The samādhi of non-contention] A samādhi without a discriminating mind, single-flavored and equal. [Free of desire] Seeking nothing, clinging to nothing. The Sutra of Forty-Two Sections says: “When the World-Honored One had accomplished the Way, he thought thus: Freedom from desire and stillness—this is the most supreme.” [Araṇya] Rendered in Chinese as “non-contention,” also called stillness. [Delighting in the practice of araṇya] Delighting in the practice of non-contention. “Delight” means to love it to the utmost, the meaning of mind and practice according with each other.
Adorning the Pure Land”—The Vimalakīrti Sutra

Chapter One, “The Buddha-Land,” says: “As the mind is purified, so all merit is purified. Therefore, Ratnākara! If a bodhisattva wishes to attain a Pure Land, he should purify his mind; as his mind is purified, so the Buddha-land is purified.” This section enters the core and sets forth the method of the mind-ground: “All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” As the mind is purified, so the Buddha-land is purified (adorning the Pure Land); freedom from marks must begin here.

The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? In the past, when the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he attain anything with respect to the Dharma? No, World-Honored One! When the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he in truth attained nothing with respect to the Dharma.
